title: Source–Sink Carbon Allocation
summary: Leaves that export photosynthate act as sources, while actively growing, storage, root, and reproductive tissues act as sinks. Source–sink strength changes with plant stage, tissue age, environment, and stress, so carbon allocation is dynamic rather than fixed.
keyConcepts: Mature photosynthetically active leaves are major carbohydrate sources
Expanding leaves, roots, meristems, flowers, and developing seeds can act as sinks
Sink strength depends on tissue demand and capacity to import and use assimilates
Stress can reduce source supply, sink demand, transport capacity, or several at once
Training and pruning change canopy structure and may alter the balance among competing sinks
measureObserve: Track which leaves are fully expanded versus still developing
Record growth rate of competing shoots and reproductive sites
Compare canopy light distribution with lower-canopy senescence
Note whether growth slows after root, water, temperature, or light stress
Use repeated observations rather than inferring carbon allocation from one plant photograph
commonMistakes: Assuming every large leaf is always a net source under all conditions
Treating pruning as a guaranteed way to redirect a fixed amount of energy
Ignoring root demand when interpreting shoot growth
Assuming larger sink number always increases total production
Using source–sink language as a substitute for measurements of light, water, and plant development
visualNeeds: Leaf age and source transition sequence

title: Stomatal Conductance & Gas Exchange
summary: Stomata regulate the exchange of carbon dioxide and water vapor between the leaf and atmosphere. Their behavior responds to light, internal carbon dioxide, water status, vapor-pressure conditions, hormones, temperature, and other signals.
keyConcepts: Carbon dioxide entry and water-vapor loss are coupled through stomatal pores
Stomatal conductance is not the same as photosynthetic rate
High atmospheric demand can increase transpiration pressure while also promoting stomatal restriction if plant water supply cannot keep pace
Leaf temperature and boundary-layer conditions change gas-exchange behavior
Root-zone stress can alter stomatal behavior before dramatic visual symptoms appear
measureObserve: Record air temperature, RH, leaf temperature, and light context together
Compare leaf posture and temperature across canopy zones
Observe recovery after irrigation or environmental transitions
Use gas-exchange instruments when quantitative stomatal conductance is required
Track root-zone moisture and EC alongside atmospheric measurements
commonMistakes: Treating a VPD number as a direct measurement of stomatal conductance
Assuming open stomata always mean optimal photosynthesis
Ignoring leaf temperature when interpreting atmospheric demand
Changing humidity without considering root water supply
Diagnosing stomatal behavior from leaf curl alone

title: Soil–Plant–Atmosphere Hydraulic Continuum
summary: Water movement through the plant is driven by gradients in water potential from the root zone through xylem to evaporating leaf surfaces and the atmosphere. The continuity of this pathway links substrate moisture, root function, stem transport, leaf temperature, and transpiration.
keyConcepts: Water moves along water-potential gradients rather than because roots simply push it upward
Root hydraulic resistance, xylem transport, leaf conductance, and atmospheric demand all influence flow
Loss of hydraulic continuity can occur under severe dehydration or vascular damage
Recovery after water stress depends on tissue condition and the severity and duration of stress
Atmospheric demand can expose root-zone limitations that are not obvious under milder conditions
measureObserve: Track substrate moisture before and after high-demand periods
Compare leaf posture at predawn, midday, and recovery periods
Record leaf and air temperature together
Inspect stems and roots when wilt persists despite adequate bulk moisture
Map recurring wilt to irrigation zones, root volumes, or vascular injury
commonMistakes: Assuming wilt always means the substrate is dry
Increasing irrigation without checking root oxygen or disease
Treating all xylem dysfunction as permanent cavitation
Ignoring local root restriction or stem injury
Interpreting one moisture reading as the entire root-zone water status

title: Osmotic Adjustment, Turgor & Cell Expansion
summary: Cell expansion depends on water uptake, osmotic conditions, cell-wall properties, and turgor. Plants can adjust cellular solute concentrations during stress, but persistent salinity or dehydration can still suppress expansion and growth.
keyConcepts: Turgor pressure supports cell expansion and tissue posture
Osmotic potential is influenced by dissolved solutes inside cells and in the root environment
High external salinity can make water acquisition more difficult even when media appears wet
Plants can accumulate compatible solutes as part of stress acclimation
Reduced expansion can appear before widespread tissue death
measureObserve: Track root-zone EC and moisture together
Compare young-tissue expansion with mature-leaf condition
Record response after irrigation and after salinity correction
Observe whether growth remains compact despite adequate light
Separate temporary loss of turgor from irreversible tissue damage
commonMistakes: Calling every wilt event simple underwatering
Ignoring EC when media is visibly moist
Assuming osmotic adjustment means plants are unaffected by salinity
Using leaf firmness alone to infer root-zone chemistry
Correcting salinity aggressively without considering root oxygen and irrigation uniformity

title: Phytochrome & Photoperiod Signaling
summary: Phytochrome photoreceptors help plants interpret red and far-red light and participate in measuring light–dark transitions. In photoperiod-sensitive cannabis, flowering behavior depends on integrated signaling over repeated daily cycles rather than on one isolated light reading.
keyConcepts: Phytochrome interconverts between light-responsive states influenced strongly by red and far-red wavelengths
Night length and interruptions can matter independently of total daily photosynthetic light
Photoperiod signaling interacts with developmental state and genotype
Brief unintended night lighting can be biologically meaningful depending on intensity, spectrum, duration, and timing
Photoperiod and DLI describe different aspects of the light environment
measureObserve: Document actual lights-on and lights-off times
Audit dark periods for leaks, work lights, indicators, and neighboring light sources
Track flowering transition across cultivars and canopy zones
Record blackout timing and environmental effects after closure
Distinguish photoperiod changes from changes in total light quantity
commonMistakes: Treating DLI and photoperiod as interchangeable
Assuming any tiny light exposure has the same biological effect
Ignoring genotype and developmental stage
Changing spectrum, intensity, and photoperiod simultaneously without records
Diagnosing delayed flowering without checking the actual dark period

title: Photomorphogenesis & Shade-Avoidance Responses
summary: Plants use light quantity, direction, and spectral cues to shape architecture. Changes in red-to-far-red balance and local shading can influence internode elongation, leaf angle, branching, and allocation without being equivalent to simple light deficiency.
keyConcepts: Photomorphogenesis refers to developmental responses to light signals, not only photosynthetic energy capture
Neighboring leaves alter both photon quantity and spectral composition
Low red-to-far-red signals can contribute to shade-avoidance responses
Architecture feeds back on future light interception
Genotype strongly influences the magnitude and form of architectural responses
measureObserve: Map internode length across canopy positions
Compare branch angles and leaf orientation before and after crowding
Measure PPFD rather than assuming shaded appearance equals low total light
Document changes in plant spacing or canopy closure
Track responses over several nodes rather than one internode
commonMistakes: Calling all stretch a lack-of-light problem
Ignoring spectral and neighbor cues
Assuming one cultivar's architecture predicts another's
Responding to elongation without checking temperature and developmental stage
Using a single top-canopy light reading to explain lower-canopy morphology

title: Auxin, Cytokinin & Branching Control
summary: Branching emerges from interactions among the shoot apex, axillary buds, vascular connections, resource status, and hormone signaling. Auxin and cytokinin are important parts of this network, but training responses should not be reduced to a single-hormone explanation.
keyConcepts: The shoot apex contributes to apical dominance through a broader signaling network
Axillary buds differ in developmental readiness and access to resources
Auxin transport, cytokinin signaling, sugars, and strigolactone-related pathways interact in bud outgrowth
Removing or repositioning the apex changes multiple signals at once
Branching response depends on plant stage, genotype, light environment, and root status
measureObserve: Record which node was topped or trained
Track bud activation and elongation over several days
Compare symmetrical branches for vigor and light exposure
Document root stress or transplant timing before interpreting weak branching
Measure canopy distribution after the response rather than only immediately after the cut
commonMistakes: Explaining topping entirely as auxin removal
Expecting every axillary bud to respond equally
Ignoring sugar supply and light exposure
Repeatedly pruning before the previous response is visible
Assuming more branches always create a better canopy

title: Gibberellins, Stem Elongation & Development
summary: Gibberellin signaling contributes to stem elongation, developmental transitions, and other growth processes. Observed stretch is the integrated outcome of hormone signaling, light, temperature, genotype, developmental stage, and resource availability.
keyConcepts: Gibberellins can promote cell elongation and growth in many plant tissues
Internode length is a phenotype produced by several interacting signals
Temperature and spectral environment can change elongation independently of total light quantity
Rapid elongation can alter mechanical support and canopy uniformity
Developmental transitions can change elongation rate even without a management change
measureObserve: Measure internode length at successive nodes
Record day and night temperature conditions
Track elongation during transition into flowering
Compare canopy zones for light and crowding
Observe stem diameter and support needs as elongation changes
commonMistakes: Calling all elongation a nutrient problem
Assuming gibberellin alone explains architecture
Using one internode as the entire plant's growth-rate indicator
Ignoring the flowering transition
Correcting stretch with severe interventions before measuring the environment

title: Ethylene, Wounding & Stress Signaling
summary: Ethylene is a gaseous plant hormone involved in responses to wounding, flooding, senescence, organ abscission, mechanical stress, and developmental processes. Its effects depend on concentration, tissue sensitivity, developmental stage, and interactions with other signals.
keyConcepts: Ethylene production can increase after wounding or other stress
Mechanical training creates both structural change and wound-response signaling
Low-oxygen root conditions can alter ethylene-related responses
Senescing tissues often show coordinated hormone and nutrient-remobilization changes
Hormone responses are networks rather than isolated switches
measureObserve: Record training, pruning, transplant, or mechanical injury events
Track wound closure and nearby tissue condition
Check root-zone aeration when abnormal swelling, epinasty, or stress is suspected
Compare damaged and undamaged branches
Observe whether symptoms continue after the original stress has ended
commonMistakes: Treating ethylene as the only explanation for any stress response
Assuming visible wound swelling is always beneficial strengthening
Ignoring root hypoxia in stress interpretation
Applying hormone terminology without documenting the triggering event
Confusing correlation with direct hormone measurement

title: Leaf Senescence & Nutrient Remobilization
summary: Leaf senescence is a regulated developmental process that dismantles cellular machinery and remobilizes useful compounds before tissue death. Stress can accelerate senescence, while normal aging can resemble nutrient or root-zone problems if location and progression are ignored.
keyConcepts: Senescence involves ordered changes in chlorophyll, proteins, membranes, and nutrient transport
Older leaves often enter senescence before younger source leaves
Nitrogen and other mobile resources can be remobilized from aging tissue
Stress-induced senescence can overlap visually with normal developmental aging
Whole-plant source–sink relationships change as reproductive demand increases
measureObserve: Map which leaves yellow first and whether the pattern is symmetrical
Record plant stage and flowering progression
Compare senescence with root-zone EC, pH, moisture, and disease observations
Track whether yellowing progresses into younger tissue
Document leaf loss and canopy light exposure over time
commonMistakes: Calling all late-cycle yellowing a deficiency
Calling all yellowing normal senescence
Ignoring root disease because the plant is in flower
Removing large amounts of aging foliage before checking what the pattern means
Using calendar week as the only maturity context

title: Abscission & Organ Shedding
summary: Plants can actively separate leaves, flowers, or other organs through specialized abscission zones. Shedding can be developmental or stress-related, so dropped tissue should be interpreted with timing, attachment-zone condition, and whole-plant context.
keyConcepts: Abscission is an active developmental separation process
Hormone balance and tissue age influence abscission-zone activation
Water stress, root injury, shading, and reproductive changes can alter organ retention
Physical breakage and true abscission leave different evidence
Dropped organs can become sanitation issues in dense canopies or production floors
measureObserve: Inspect the attachment point of shed organs
Record whether shedding is localized or whole-plant
Compare shaded interior leaves with well-lit leaves
Track irrigation or root stress before shedding events
Remove fallen tissue and note recurrence
commonMistakes: Treating every dropped leaf as mechanical damage
Assuming organ shedding always indicates a nutrient shortage
Ignoring canopy shade and normal developmental turnover
Leaving fallen tissue to accumulate during disease-prone conditions
Inferring a hormone concentration from appearance alone

title: Carbon–Nitrogen Balance & Growth Allocation
summary: Plant growth depends on coordination between carbon captured through photosynthesis and nitrogen used to build proteins, nucleic acids, pigments, enzymes, and new tissues. Excess or shortage of either resource can shift growth patterns, but a simple carbon-to-nitrogen ratio does not diagnose plant health by itself.
keyConcepts: Carbon capture and nitrogen assimilation are metabolically interconnected
Nitrogen status influences leaf area, chlorophyll, enzyme capacity, and growth
High carbon supply cannot compensate for severe mineral or root limitations
Excessive nitrogen can change architecture and tissue composition without guaranteeing faster useful growth
Developmental stage changes the balance of vegetative and reproductive demand
measureObserve: Track leaf color and growth rate with root-zone EC and nutrient records
Compare new and old tissue rather than relying on one leaf
Record biomass allocation to leaves, stems, roots, and flowers when conducting trials
Use tissue analysis when precise nutrient status is required
Relate responses to light and temperature context
commonMistakes: Using dark green color as proof of ideal nitrogen status
Assuming more nitrogen always increases productive growth
Ignoring light limitation when growth remains weak
Treating carbon–nitrogen concepts as a fertilizer recipe
Comparing plants at different developmental stages without normalization
visualNeeds: Nitrogen status and canopy response comparison

title: Reproductive Source–Sink Transition
summary: As flowering progresses, expanding inflorescences and developing reproductive tissues become major sinks. The plant's allocation pattern changes alongside canopy aging, root activity, light interception, and reproductive development.
keyConcepts: Flowering changes the distribution of growth demand across the plant
Reproductive sinks compete with continued vegetative growth and root maintenance
Lower-canopy leaves may contribute differently depending on light exposure and tissue age
Pollination and seed development can alter sink demand within flowers
Late-cycle decline can reflect development, stress, disease, or combinations and should be separated with evidence
measureObserve: Track flower expansion and branch growth simultaneously
Map canopy light interception as flowers increase in size
Record lower-leaf senescence and root-zone condition together
Compare pollinated and unpollinated sites when relevant
Use repeated maturity observations rather than one late-cycle snapshot
commonMistakes: Assuming flowering stops all vegetative metabolism
Treating every lower-leaf decline as normal fade
Ignoring root health late in flower
Assuming pollination affects only seed presence and not resource allocation
Using calendar week alone to infer reproductive demand

title: Trichome Secretion & Secondary Metabolism
summary: Glandular trichomes are specialized structures associated with the production and storage of many secondary metabolites in cannabis. Their abundance, development, and chemistry reflect genotype, tissue type, developmental stage, and environment rather than one simple cultivation variable.
keyConcepts: Secretory cells in glandular trichomes contribute to cannabinoid and terpene biosynthesis
Trichome density and metabolite concentration are related but not interchangeable measurements
Different tissues and trichome types can have different chemical profiles
Developmental stage changes trichome structure and chemistry
Environmental responses can influence secondary metabolism but should not be reduced to universal stress recipes
measureObserve: Standardize tissue type and sampling position
Use consistent magnification for structural comparisons
Separate trichome density observations from chemical potency testing
Track developmental stage when comparing samples
Use laboratory analysis when cannabinoid or terpene concentration matters
commonMistakes: Equating visible frost with a precise potency value
Comparing sugar leaves directly with flower bracts without noting tissue type
Assuming amber trichomes provide a complete chemical profile
Using stress as a blanket recommendation to increase secondary metabolites
Treating microscope appearance as a substitute for analytical chemistry

title: Respiration, Temperature & Carbon Cost
summary: Respiration supplies usable energy and metabolic intermediates by consuming stored carbon. Temperature strongly affects respiration rate within biological limits, so warm conditions can increase carbon costs even when photosynthetic light is unchanged.
keyConcepts: Respiration occurs in living tissues day and night
Higher temperature often increases metabolic reaction rates until stress or damage alters the response
Night temperature can influence carbon balance independently of daytime PPFD
Roots, stems, leaves, flowers, and growing tissues all have respiratory costs
Net biomass gain reflects carbon captured minus carbon used for respiration and other losses
measureObserve: Record day and night temperatures separately
Track growth rate during sustained warm-night periods
Compare root-zone temperature with canopy temperature
Relate temperature shifts to light availability and plant stage
Use controlled comparisons rather than assuming a single optimal night temperature
commonMistakes: Treating nighttime temperature as irrelevant because photosynthesis stops
Assuming warmer always means faster productive growth
Ignoring root respiration and root-zone temperature
Comparing biomass without considering temperature history
Using respiration concepts to justify extreme temperature swings
